Rule 8(f) also applies when a small craft is near a channel-bound vessel.

TP: Rule 8(f) exists to prevent a vessel from impeding the safe passage of another vessel.
Rule 8(f) applies in situations such as crossing a Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) lane.
Rule 8(f) also applies when a small craft is near a channel-bound vessel.
FN: Rule 8 subparagraph f ensures a vessel that is not to impede another takes early action to leave sufficient sea room
Rule 8 subparagraph f ensures a vessel that is not to impede another does not force the right-of-way vessel into a late reactive manoeuvre
Rule 8 subparagraph f clarifies that if risk of collision nonetheless develops the normal steering and sailing rule obligations still fully apply
Rule 8 subparagraph f clarifies that Section II give-way duties still fully apply if risk of collision develops
Rule 8 subparagraph f bridges the not to impede concept used in Rules 9, 10, and 18 with the general good-seamanship obligations of Rule 8

statements: A 9-metre open motorboat is underway at night.
A 9-metre open motorboat shows a single all-round white light only.
The display of a single all-round white light only is not compliant with maritime navigation rules.

TP: A 9-metre open motorboat is underway at night.
A 9-metre open motorboat shows a single all-round white light only.
FP: The display of a single all-round white light only is not compliant with maritime navigation rules.
FN: A 9-metre open motorboat underway at night showing a single all-round white light only is compliant
Rule 23 subparagraph c permits an all-round white light in lieu of masthead light and sternlight for vessels under 12 metres
Rule 23 subparagraph d clause i allows a vessel under 7 metres with maximum speed not exceeding 7 knots to show simply an all-round white light
Rule 23 subparagraphs c and d provide tiered simplified lighting options for small power-driven vessels

statements: Rule 17 pertains to stand-on vessel duties when vessels are in sight of one another.
Rule 19 applies to vessels navigating in restricted visibility.
A vessel cannot simply 'stand on' in fog because visibility is limited, increasing the risk of collision.
In restricted visibility, vessels must take appropriate action to avoid collisions, which may include altering course or speed.

TP: Rule 17 pertains to stand-on vessel duties when vessels are in sight of one another.
Rule 19 applies to vessels navigating in restricted visibility.
A vessel cannot simply 'stand on' in fog because visibility is limited, increasing the risk of collision.
In restricted visibility, vessels must take appropriate action to avoid collisions, which may include altering course or speed.
FN: Rule 17 stand-on concept depends on visual confirmation that the give-way vessel is aware of and responding to the situation
Visual confirmation that the give-way vessel is aware of and responding to the situation is unavailable in restricted visibility
Rule 19 imposes mutual proactive avoiding-action duties on all vessels detected only by radar
Rule 19 does not provide a passive hold course and speed role
This contrast between Rule 17 and Rule 19 is one of the most frequently tested conceptual distinctions in COLREG exams

statements: Annex I requires a minimum vertical separation between a vessel's two masthead lights only on vessels above a certain length.
The specific length threshold for vessels requiring the minimum vertical separation is not provided in the answer.

TP: Annex I requires a minimum vertical separation between a vessel's two masthead lights only on vessels above a certain length.
FP: The specific length threshold for vessels requiring the minimum vertical separation is not provided in the answer.
FN: Smaller vessels have limited mast height and structural capacity to achieve large vertical separations
The generally shorter length and lower speed of smaller vessels reduces the practical need for the same degree of aspect-differentiation precision required for large fast vessels at greater ranges
Annex I scales its technical requirements to vessel size throughout balancing safety benefit against practicability

statements: A sailing vessel underway in fog sounds one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts every two minutes.
The sound signal described is compliant with Rule 35.
Rule 35 pertains to sound signals in restricted visibility.

TP: A sailing vessel underway in fog sounds one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts every two minutes.
The sound signal described is compliant with Rule 35.
Rule 35 pertains to sound signals in restricted visibility.
FN: A sailing vessel underway in fog sounding one prolonged followed by two short blasts every two minutes is compliant with Rule 35
Rule 35 subparagraph c prescribes one prolonged plus two short blasts at intervals of not more than 2 minutes for a sailing vessel underway
The fog signal interval must be not more than 2 minutes
Rule 35 subparagraph c groups sailing vessels with NUC, RAM, CBD, fishing, and towing or pushing vessels underway for this common fog signal

statements: Two power-driven vessels are approaching each other.
Each vessel sees the other fine on her own bow.
The relative bearing offset from dead ahead is a few degrees.
This situation should be treated as head-on.

TP: Two power-driven vessels are approaching each other.
Each vessel sees the other fine on her own bow.
The relative bearing offset from dead ahead is a few degrees.
This situation should be treated as head-on.
FN: This situation should be treated as head-on under Rule 14
Rule 14 subparagraph c requires that if there is any doubt whether a head-on situation exists it shall be assumed that it does
A near-dead-ahead sighting with only a slight offset falls within the doubt requiring head-on assumption
This prevents mariners from exploiting small bearing offsets to claim a crossing situation instead of the mutual head-on obligation

statements: A vessel engaged in diving operations from a small craft displays the rigid replica of the International Code flag 'A' ('Alpha').
The full Rule 27(b) RAM lights/shapes are not exhibited by the small craft.
The International Code flag 'A' ('Alpha') is an internationally recognised signal for vessels engaged in diving operations.

TP: A vessel engaged in diving operations from a small craft displays the rigid replica of the International Code flag 'A' ('Alpha').
The full Rule 27(b) RAM lights/shapes are not exhibited by the small craft.
The International Code flag 'A' ('Alpha') is an internationally recognised signal for vessels engaged in diving operations.
FN: The Alpha flag is widely used and recognised in many jurisdictions to indicate a diver down
The Alpha flag is not itself a Rule 27 light or shape substitute under COLREG

statements: A vessel may not anchor in a narrow channel under Rule 9(g).
Rule 9(g) states that vessels shall not anchor in a narrow channel.

TP: A vessel may not anchor in a narrow channel under Rule 9(g).
Rule 9(g) states that vessels shall not anchor in a narrow channel.
FN: A vessel wanting to anchor in a narrow channel to wait for a berth is permitted only if circumstances of the case do not admit avoiding it

Waiting for a berth is not itself an exception to the prohibition on anchoring in narrow channels
A vessel waiting for a berth should seek to anchor outside the channel if practicable
Rule 9 subparagraph g sets a strong presumption against anchoring in narrow channels

statements: Vessel A is power-driven.

Vessel B is on the starboard side of Vessel A.

Both vessels are in sight of each other.
The weather is clear.
Vessel A is the give-way vessel.
Vessel A must take action to avoid collision.

TP: Vessel A is the give-way vessel under Rule 15

Vessel A must take early and substantial action under Rule 16
